set.stem: A 65-year-old man has a 4-week history of general malaise and lethargy. Two courses of antibiotics have temporarily improved his symptoms, but overall he continues to deteriorate, and his GP notes that he has become anaemic. He is admitted with fever; blood cultures are taken and an echocardiogram shows a mass on the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely to grow from his blood cultures?
set.explanation: An indolent, weeks-long illness with anaemia and partial response to antibiotics is the picture of subacute native-valve endocarditis, classically caused by viridans streptococci from the mouth. Staphylococcus aureus causes an acute, rapidly destructive illness, S. epidermidis mainly infects prosthetic material, and enterococci (formerly Streptococcus faecalis) and S. gallolyticus are linked to genitourinary and colonic sources. Intermittent antibiotic courses before cultures are a common cause of culture-negative endocarditis, so cultures must precede antibiotics.

set.stem: A 65-year-old man with a 4-week illness of malaise, anaemia and fever has a mitral valve mass on echocardiography. Before the blood culture results are known, a junior doctor examines him for signs of endocarditis. Which of the following is the commonest finding?
set.explanation: Microscopic haematuria, from immune-complex glomerulonephritis or renal emboli, is found in a large proportion of patients with endocarditis and is more common than the classic peripheral stigmata. Splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Roth spots and conjunctival haemorrhages each occur in only a minority (roughly 5–15%) and are non-specific. Urine dipstick is therefore a simple, useful bedside test in suspected endocarditis.

A new or changing regurgitant murmur reflects valve destruction by vegetations and, with fever, is the most suggestive clinical feature of endocarditis; new valvular regurgitation on echo is a major Duke criterion. Erythema marginatum belongs to rheumatic fever, juxta-articular nodules to syphilis/yaws or rheumatic disease, and atrial fibrillation and lymphadenopathy are non-specific. Blood cultures and echocardiography should follow.

set.stem: A 35-year-old man who injects drugs has night sweats and weight loss. He is febrile (38.5 °C) and infective endocarditis is suspected. Which organism is most likely responsible?
set.explanation: In people who inject drugs, Staphylococcus aureus from the skin is by far the commonest cause of endocarditis, typically affecting the tricuspid valve and causing septic pulmonary emboli. Oral streptococci (S. mutans, S. sanguinis) follow dental bacteraemia, Enterococcus faecalis genitourinary or bowel sources, and Coxiella burnetii causes culture-negative endocarditis after animal exposure. Empirical therapy should therefore cover S. aureus, including MRSA where prevalent.

why: Same idea as peri-0070 (endocarditis after dental extraction → oral viridans streptococci); this version also has two viridans streptococci as options

set.stem: A 40-year-old man with an underlying cardiac condition is about to have root canal treatment and a new crown fitted. For which of the following conditions is antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis recommended?
set.explanation: Current ESC and AHA guidance restricts dental prophylaxis to the highest-risk patients – prosthetic valves or valve repair material, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease (or repair with prosthetic material in the last 6 months or with residual shunt) and ventricular assist devices – before procedures that manipulate the gingiva or root apex. An atrial or ventricular septal defect, previous CABG and a pacemaker are not in this group, so none of the listed patients needs prophylaxis; NICE advises against routine prophylaxis altogether. Good oral hygiene and regular dental review are recommended for all.

set.stem: Some clinical features of infective endocarditis result from immune-complex deposition. Which of the following is NOT an immune-complex phenomenon?
set.explanation: The immunological phenomena of endocarditis (a minor Duke criterion) are Osler's nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis and a positive rheumatoid factor. A splenic abscess results from septic embolism with infarction and infection, i.e. a vascular/embolic phenomenon, like Janeway lesions, conjunctival haemorrhages, mycotic aneurysms and septic infarcts. Persistent fever despite antibiotics with left upper quadrant pain should prompt imaging for splenic abscess.

why: Original distractors included Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages, which are also embolic/vascular rather than immune-complex phenomena (three correct answers); replaced by glomerulonephritis and rheumatoid factor
Same idea and level as peri-0016 (suspected endocarditis → blood cultures are the key diagnostic test)

set.stem: A previously well 45-year-old man has fevers and malaise. He has multiple splinter haemorrhages and a systolic murmur, and infective endocarditis is suspected. Regarding the modified Duke criteria, which statement is INCORRECT?
options: The presence of Osler's nodes is a minor criterion
A positive rheumatoid factor is a minor criterion
Echocardiographic evidence of new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve is a major criterion
A single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or a phase I IgG titre > 1:800 is a major criterion
A definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
set.explanation: A definite clinical diagnosis by the modified Duke criteria requires two major criteria, one major plus three minor, or five minor criteria; three minor criteria give only a 'possible' diagnosis (as does one major plus one minor). Osler's nodes and rheumatoid factor are immunological minor criteria, and new prosthetic dehiscence and Coxiella burnetii (single culture or phase I IgG > 1:800) are major criteria. Pathological demonstration of vegetations or abscess also confirms endocarditis.

why: One option was an incomplete fragment (no statement); rewritten as a correct statement about Coxiella serology, key unchanged

set.explanation: Subacute endocarditis on a previously abnormal valve (mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation) after a dental extraction is most likely due to viridans streptococci from the oral flora, which enter the blood during gingival manipulation. Staphylococcus aureus follows skin, line or injecting sources and runs a more acute course, enterococci follow genitourinary or bowel procedures, and Candida and Pseudomonas are seen with prosthetic material, lines or injecting drug use. Benzylpenicillin (with gentamicin in some regimens) is effective for sensitive strains.

why: Same vignette and question as peri-0082 (acute rheumatic fever → antistreptolysin O titre)

set.stem: A 12-year-old girl has high fever and swelling of the left ankle and knee 3 weeks after a sore throat. Two years ago she developed breathlessness and a generalised rash when given dicloxacillin for a skin infection. Temperature 38.8 °C, pulse 87/min, BP 98/62 mmHg. The left ankle and knee are swollen and tender with limited movement, and a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
set.explanation: This is acute rheumatic fever (arthritis and carditis after streptococcal pharyngitis), and antibiotics are given to eradicate residual group A streptococci and then as secondary prophylaxis. Penicillin or amoxicillin is first choice, but she had an anaphylactic-type reaction to a penicillin, so a macrolide such as clarithromycin or azithromycin is used. Vancomycin, doxycycline and ciprofloxacin are not appropriate for streptococcal eradication; high-dose aspirin or naproxen treats the arthritis.

why: Asked for 'most appropriate pharmacotherapy', which could also be aspirin/NSAID; stem now asks for the antibiotic
Same idea and level as peri-0016 (suspected endocarditis → blood cultures confirm the diagnosis)
Same PreTest question as valv-0046 (which patient benefits from dental prophylaxis → prosthetic aortic valve)

set.stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV who injects drugs presents with fever, night sweats and a holosystolic murmur that increases on inspiration. Which complication of his condition is most likely?
options: Painful nodules on the finger pads
Painless haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles
set.explanation: Endocarditis in people who inject drugs usually involves the tricuspid valve (a holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration), and fragments of vegetation embolise to the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli, seen in up to three-quarters of cases as multiple cavitating nodules. Splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots are manifestations of left-sided, systemic-circulation disease and are much less common in isolated right-sided infection. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism.

why: 'Pulmonary embolism' specified as septic pulmonary emboli and a tricuspid (inspiratory) murmur added so the right-sided answer is unambiguous
Same idea as peri-0064 (right-sided/injecting-drug-use endocarditis → Staphylococcus aureus)

set.stem: A 34-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has fatigue, exertional breathlessness, low-grade fevers and splinter haemorrhages. He was started on empirical IV vancomycin, and blood cultures now grow Cardiobacterium hominis. What is the next step in management?
set.explanation: Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK organism (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) – slow-growing Gram-negative bacilli that may produce beta-lactamase. Once identified, therapy is switched to a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (6 for prosthetic valves). Vancomycin and cefazolin lack reliable Gram-negative activity, ampicillin may be inactivated by beta-lactamase, and gentamicin monotherapy is inappropriate.

set.stem: A 64-year-old man admitted 7 days ago with pancreatitis after abdominal trauma develops fever, breathlessness and a new holosystolic murmur. There is purulent discharge from his central venous catheter site. Which organism is most likely responsible?
set.explanation: Healthcare-associated endocarditis, particularly from infected intravascular catheters, is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, which causes acute destructive valve infection; the purulent line site points to it. Streptococcus gallolyticus is linked with colonic neoplasia, Haemophilus aphrophilus is a slow-growing HACEK organism, and Gram-negatives such as Pseudomonas and Klebsiella are uncommon causes of endocarditis. Remove the line, take blood cultures and give anti-staphylococcal therapy (vancomycin until MRSA is excluded).

why: The same Other Sources question (injecting drug user with holosystolic murmur → septic pulmonary emboli) is printed twice

set.stem: At autopsy, multiple small sterile nodules composed of immune complexes, fibrin and thrombus are found on both surfaces of the mitral valve, including the ventricular side. In which patient would these findings most likely be found?
options: A 71-year-old man with acute high fever and nail-bed haemorrhages
A 41-year-old woman with a facial rash and non-erosive arthritis
A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman who injects drugs
A 6-year-old girl with subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum
set.explanation: Sterile verrucous vegetations on both sides of the valve leaflets, especially the ventricular surface of the mitral valve, are Libman–Sacks (non-bacterial) endocarditis of systemic lupus erythematosus, suggested here by a malar rash and non-erosive arthritis; antiphospholipid antibodies increase the risk. Rheumatic fever produces small vegetations along the lines of closure on the atrial surface, while infective endocarditis (acute S. aureus, post-dental streptococcal, or injecting drug use) produces bacterial vegetations. Libman–Sacks lesions may embolise or cause regurgitation.

set.stem: Three weeks after a transurethral resection of the prostate, a 70-year-old man has fever, malaise and limb pain. He has subungual petechiae, tender red papules on the fingers and a new holosystolic murmur. Blood cultures grow a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus. Which organism is most likely responsible?
set.explanation: Endocarditis after a urological procedure in an older man is typical of enterococci, and a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus that grows in chains identifies Enterococcus faecalis. Staphylococci are catalase-positive clusters, Streptococcus gallolyticus is PYR-negative and associated with colorectal cancer, and Haemophilus aphrophilus is a Gram-negative HACEK organism. Treatment is amoxicillin combined with ceftriaxone or gentamicin for about 6 weeks.

set.stem: An 18-year-old man has fever and flitting pain in both knees and elbows; the right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the previous week. He has a low-grade fever, a grade III/VI high-pitched apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla and a soft mid-diastolic murmur at the base. A tender nodule is felt over an extensor tendon of the hand, and there are pink erythematous lesions on the abdomen, some with central clearing. Haematocrit 0.42, WBC 12 × 10⁹/L (80% neutrophils, 20% lymphocytes), ESR 60 mm/h. His ECG is shown. Which test is most critical to the diagnosis?
set.explanation: Migratory polyarthritis, carditis (mitral regurgitation), subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum with a raised ESR and a prolonged PR interval on the ECG (shown) fulfil the Jones criteria, which also require evidence of recent group A streptococcal infection – most practically a raised or rising antistreptolysin O (or anti-DNase B) titre. Blood cultures help exclude endocarditis, and echocardiography documents valvulitis, but neither proves rheumatic fever. ANA (lupus) and creatine kinase (myositis) do not fit this picture.

A prolonged PR interval is a minor Jones criterion for acute rheumatic fever and is not part of the modified Duke criteria (although new conduction block in endocarditis may signal an aortic root abscess). Positive Coxiella burnetii serology is a major criterion, fever over 38 °C and Roth spots are minor criteria, and microbiology or histology of vegetations or embolic material is a pathological criterion that confirms the diagnosis. Definite endocarditis needs two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor criteria.

set.stem: A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. She had an aortic valve replacement 2 years ago. According to current ESC guidance, what antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended before this procedure?
set.explanation: A prosthetic heart valve places her in the highest-risk group, and ESC (2023) and AHA guidance recommend a single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally (or IV) 30–60 minutes before dental procedures that involve gingival manipulation or perforation of the oral mucosa, such as extraction. Chlorhexidine mouthwash and phenoxymethylpenicillin are not recommended regimens, and IV co-amoxiclav is unnecessary. UK NICE guidance differs and advises against routine prophylaxis, but all guidelines stress good oral hygiene.

why: Source key (hygiene advice only) follows UK NICE; ESC/AHA recommend oral amoxicillin for prosthetic valves – stem now specifies ESC guidance, consistent with the other prophylaxis items

set.explanation: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) endocarditis is strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia, so it is the most likely organism in a patient with colorectal cancer, and its isolation in any patient should prompt colonoscopy. Viridans streptococci follow a dental source, Staphylococcus epidermidis mainly infects prosthetic material, and Brucella and Coxiella cause culture-negative endocarditis after animal exposure. Aortic valve vegetations with regurgitation also need early surgical assessment.

set.stem: A 60-year-old man who had a mitral valve replacement 3 years ago presents acutely with high fever, rigors and fatigue 1 week after a large boil (furuncle) on his thigh. Echocardiography shows a new vegetation on the prosthetic valve, and three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be responsible?
set.explanation: Late prosthetic valve endocarditis (more than a year after surgery) has a spectrum similar to native-valve infection, and an acute illness following a furuncle points to Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest cause of endocarditis in high-income settings. Coagulase-negative staphylococci dominate early prosthetic infection acquired at surgery, S. gallolyticus is linked to colorectal cancer, enterococci to genitourinary procedures, and Candida to lines and immunosuppression. S. aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis has a high mortality and usually needs rifampicin-containing therapy and early surgery.

why: At 4 months after surgery (early PVE, within 1 year per ESC) coagulase-negative staphylococci were equally defensible and 'Staphylococcus bovis' was misnamed; timeline and a skin source added, options revised
